My partner and I are in our mid twenties and have children together. While at university, I developed a friendship with a lab/project partner that made my SO feel uncomfortable from the start. Due to some stress from school/moving/life, we were fighting a bit then anyway and I foolishly ignored their feelings, even explicitly telling them I'll work with whomever I want.

Long story short, my friend started coming on to me; touching inappropriately, inviting me to use their bed after an all night study session (I was too dumb to realize this wasn't just a friendly offer, but not dumb enough to do it), etc.. I was too dense (and in denial) to pick up the obvious hints until the touching got very intimate (deliberate and lingering touch on my upper thigh) and around two years had passed. During these 2 years, I was open with my SO about the stuff my friend did and dismissed their objections and concerns as just being jealous. At this point they were convinced of emotional infidelity and strongly suspected sexual too.

Once I'd realized that my friend did have an interest I stopped spending any personal time together, apologized to my SO for not listening, and cut contact with my friend once we complete a semester project that we'd already started. My SO didn't like that I finished the project with this person, but it was a necessary evil to ensure graduation, in my opinion.

I graduated before my friend, got a job, and everything was looking up in my relationship. Then I hear from a manager at my company that my friend is seeking a job here (where they knew I worked), and asked my opinion of the candidate since they mentioned working with me. I didn't want to rock the boat and be the dramatic person at work, so I gave a tepid review and dropped it. Nothing seems to come of it but apparently my friend kept trying because around nine months after that manager approached me, I hear that my friend is starting on the same project as me soon.

My SO was understandingly unhappy. They had wanted me to confront my friend directly all along and I avoided it because I don't like confrontation. I finally contacted my friend and, for the first time, told them I didn't appreciate their advances at school and that we won't be friends when they start work. I got a weak apology sprinkled with lies and evasions but since showing up at work their behavior has been mostly professional. There were some early probing questions to see if I really meant it and a couple inappropriate sexual remarks made on a business trip together, but no more touching or getting too personal.

The problem is that my SO has strong doubts about my fidelity (I never cheated) and is concerned about me working with this person, especially traveling together. What's my best path forward? How can I put my SO's worries at ease? I really don't want to give up the job; it's a really good one and it seems unfair to be chased out by the person who caused this.

Edit: I'll gladly answer your questions if you think I left anything important out. But for privacy reasons, I don't disclose my sex or orientation. If deemed necessary for a good answer, I may disclose SO's and friend's sexes since both are switch hitters, so to speak.
I made my partner think I had an affair. How do I fix things?

I've had a similar situation happen to me before where my gf got it in her head that I was cheating on her with my lab partner. I never cheated, and I tried lots of stuff to get her to believe me, but none of it worked and we eventually broke up because of this.

I just think that no matter what you do, you cannot force anyone's feelings to change. This extends to an SO's feelings that you've cheated. Once they get that idea in their head, it's incredibly difficult to get that idea back out of their head.
Anything you tried that didn't work well or that you'd have done differently if you knew what you do now?

Ultimately I cut all contact with my lab partner once the semester ended (at the request of my gf), but that didn't even work. In hindsight, I regret doing this because it strained a friendship that I later realized I valued quite a lot. After my gf broke up with me (total of 3 months of no contact with lab partner), I ran into my lab partner at the gym. I apologized to her for cutting her off with no explanation, and she accepted my apology. My lab partner and I became very good friends after that. We even dated for a while but it didn't work out. She's still one of my best friends though.

I hope that this answers your question. I know what it's like to feel helpless in your situation and it really sucks.

Thanks for taking the time to answer. This is a really serious issue in my life and you've been helpful.

I think, unfortunately, you're right that there's not much I can do other than act in good faith and leave it up to my SO. They'll either be able to forgive me and move on or not. It wish I knew the best course of action to take to improve my odds though.

The best course of action is whatever you think it is. Trust your own judgement.

I hope everything works out for you, relationships aren't easy but in my opinion they're absolutely worth it.

At the very least, you can learn from your mistakes.

Playing with someone's emotions in such a way as you did can carry severe consequences. They had concerns, and you dismissed them instead of putting their feelings at the same level of importance as your own.

Thanks for pointing it out. You're absolutely right. That's been the number one thing I learned from all this.

Explaining that I've learned this and promising to apply it in the future has been one of my primary damage control methods.

To be honest, and not having any intention of judging you, because I can be incredibly dense about such signs myself, if you read just the bare facts without detailed explanation, it doesn't sound very encouraging.

You work with this friend, they come on to you, you ignore it, they come on to you more including touching you inappropriately, make suggestions, invite you to sleep with them during an all-nighter, and basically make quite obvious their intentions, for TWO YEARS. I perfectly believe that you just didn't see this happening, but unless your SO thinks you're a moron, there's got to be some suspicion that you aren't as ignorant of this attention as you protest.

Then they join you in your job when you even had the chance to block their employment, and the two of you work on projects and go on business trips together, after you've made it clear that you are now aware of their intentions to you and everyone knows what game is afoot.

I think, having typed up this synopsis, that the problem is the apparent difference between what you say and what it appears has happened. If you were to be on the outside of your working relationship with this friend, as your SO is, you talk a lot about your innocence, but when you get decisions to really stall any further interaction, you don't take them.

So some questions, can you change projects to work with someone else, can you consider changing departments, or even jobs? MAybe just offering to do one or all of these things to satisfy your SO's suspicions may be enough, the offer being sufficient to emphasise the priority you give their feelings and upset.

All this narrows down to, how far are you prepared to go to squash these suspicions, because anytime you stay working with this friend may not make things worse, but they certainly won't make things better.
